q7.answer: The API generates the 32-byte token, base64url-encodes it, and builds the link. The raw token goes only into the email job payload, which is encrypted at rest and is sent by the worker through the mail provider. Only the SHA-256 hash is written to password_reset_tokens, and the payload is deleted once the job is sent or dropped.

q8.answer: On open, the API computes sha256(T) and looks up the row by token_hash through the unique index. The link is good only if used_at and revoked_at are both null and expires_at is later than now(). Otherwise the user sees the expired page, and nothing is written.

q9.answer: The count lives in the password_reset_tokens table itself: it counts the account's rows with created_at within the last 60 minutes, and the count runs while the request holds the row lock on the user's users row. Rows fall out of the window as time passes, and the cleanup job deletes rows older than 60 minutes, so the table holds only what the cap needs.

q10.answer: When a new link is issued, inside the same transaction and only after the count check passes (under 3), the API sets revoked_at on all of the account's active tokens before it inserts the new token and commits. Earlier links are not touched on open or on reset.

q11.answer: In one transaction, the API updates users.password_hash, sets used_at on this token and on all the user's other unused tokens, deletes the user's sessions rows, and inserts the 'password changed' email job, then commits. The notice job is queued inside that transaction, so it commits with the reset and the worker sends it afterwards. The hash is computed before the transaction starts.

q12.answer: The submit transaction runs SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the token row, so the second request waits for the first to commit or roll back. After the lock is acquired, the transaction checks again that the token is active. The first request sets used_at and commits. The second finds it used, rolls back, and shows the expired page, so only one password change commits.
